claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by atomic size mismatch and the resulting lattice strain.
Atomic size mismatch produces lattice strain in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Lattice strain controls whether the alloy remains disordered or segregates into ordered intermetallic compounds.
A composition near an optimal balance of atomic sizes and configurational entropy can form a nominally single-phase, disordered Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy.
Changing Al or other elemental proportions modulates atomic size mismatch and associated lattice strain.
Atomic size differences generate local lattice distortions and strain fields.
Local lattice distortions and strain fields promote nucleation of short-range ordering and intermetallic phases.
Below a critical atomic-size-mismatch threshold, configurational entropy dominates and maintains a single-phase disordered structure.
The single-phase disordered structure provides high toughness, environmental resistance, and radiation tolerance.
Above the critical mismatch threshold, increased strain energy drives a transition to ordered intermetallic phases.
Formation of ordered intermetallic phases degrades high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness.
Compositions below the critical mismatch threshold will retain a stable disordered microstructure.
Compositions below the critical mismatch threshold will retain high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
Compositions with greater atomic size mismatch will form secondary ordered phases, potentially including B2-type ordering.
Greater atomic size mismatch and secondary ordering will reduce the targeted properties relative to the baseline.
A standard Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni composition with moderate Al content has an optimal balance of size mismatch and configurational entropy and is single-phase and disordered.

contradictions.description: The stated boundary limits the hypothesis to the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system, whereas the proposed substitution of one element with another could change the alloy into a different elemental system unless substitution is restricted to varying proportions of the five named elements.
